question.problem:
In **ascending order**, the **exact** values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for integrals for  $f(x)={x}^{2}+2x$ on the interval $[-3,3]$ are

$c=$
{{field-1}} $\,$ and $\,c=$
{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
Applying the mean value theorem for integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c)(b-a) & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ f(c) & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3-(-3)}{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}+2x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{6}\cdot (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{x}^{2})|}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[(\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}+{3}^{2})-(\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}+(-3)^{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot [(9+9)-(-9+9)] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot 18 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the expression for $f(x)$ to solve for the value of $c:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(c) & =3 \\ {c}^{2}+2c & =3 \\ {c}^{2}+2c-3 & =0 \\ (c+1)^{2}-4 & =0 \\ c+1 & =\pm 2 \\ c & =-3,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem on the interval $[-3,3]$ are 

$$
c=-3,\,\text{and}\,c=1.
$$
